You just need to register once. Then you will (well, should) receive a new voter card each year. If you move within a county, you just need to update your address with the registrar. If you move out of the county, however, you DO need to register again, in your new county, and (if you're being good and nice) send a letter to your old county telling them that you've moved, so they can remove you from the voter roll.

The voter cards are usually mailed in January, IIRC, but things have been all screwy because of the redistricting stuff going on, so I know they were late this year. If you don't receive one for whatever reason, you can call the Secretary of State, but you don't NEED the card to vote - you can always just show your driver's license, if you have one.

Hope that helps. Let me know if you have any other questions! And thanks for voting!

Each state has a different schedule for tallying early votes and absentee ballots. Some states allow early and mail ballots to be counted as they're received, and others don't start counting until election day. 

Some states only offer 1 or 2 days of early voting and others offer a couple of weeks. 

Even within a state, some counties use paper ballots and others don't.

It's all so decentralized for political reasons, and that's why the results take time.

Returning your ballot in person:

You can return your ballot in person no later than 8 p.m. on Election Day to *the election office that sent your ballot.* You can drop off ballots for up to three other voters. You will need to show identification with name and signature when returning a ballot for someone else. Some voters may also return it in one of the designated ballot drop box locations. You may *not* drop your ballot off at your polling place on election day.

The following is from the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana.

*Under strict scrutiny, a law must pass three tests to be considered valid. The
government first must prove it has a compelling interest that justifies the passage
of the law. In the case of gun laws, public safety is the state’s compelling
interest. Courts generally agree that public safety is a compelling interest or
a valid reason for states to pass laws that might infringe on an individual’s
Second Amendment rights.
The law also must be narrowly tailored to achieve the compelling interest.
That is, the law may not be overly broad in its reach. For example, a law that
bans any individual with a misdemeanor conviction from purchasing a gun
for the rest of his life would be considered excessively broad as compared to
a similar ban for an individual convicted of a violent crime.
Finally, the law must also be the least restrictive means of achieving the
state’s compelling interest. If there is any alternative that is less restrictive
but would still achieve the compelling interest then the law must be judged
invalid and overturned.*

Bennwalton - 

> The sale of this clearly under-regulated "suicide kit" in a dystopian film isn't a comment on suicide, it's simply something to reinforce the fact that this is, indeed, a dystopia.

Precisely. I don't think Children of Men is a commentary on assisted suicide. But here's the interesting thing. Incidentally, the film comments on it by folding it within a network of death-dealing and despair. This "landscape of doom" stands in utter contrast to Theo, Kee, and her child - which stand opposed to the entire landscape and transform it. Quietus, after meeting Kee's child, looks quite like a different option. There is truly something to live for. That was what I was trying to bring out in the article.

> Not to mention the immense differences between a terminally ill patient and the society Theo and Kee live in. Living with a terminal illness and saving a pregnant woman from terrorists have virtually nothing in common. I understand the direction of the metaphor, but it falls apart immediately.

As long as you understand the metaphor, I'm happy. It's not meant to be an equation, but an analogy. Of course some aspects are different. But what interests me is what's similar. And what's similar, as far as I can tell, is what I outlined above and in the article - namely, that we have a "landscape of doom" - of certain imminent death and of death-dealing despair. This dystopian landscape robs the nuanced portrayls of assisted suicide in Million Dollar Baby and The Sea Inside of their raw emotion. Someone commented that I was being "emotional" with this article. I think just the opposite. I think "Children of Men" strips down the act, bare-naked so to speak, so that we can see what it is and what "sort" of act it most essentially is (i.e., its motivations, its inherent nature, and its consequences).

> I do not believe in god and do not believe in the afterlife- why should someone else's beliefs affect what happens in the (hypothetical) hospital bed I've been in for years?

They shouldn't. Belief in God is a personal matter, and no one should put their beliefs on someone else. But as I pointed out to another person, there are very good non-religious arguments made against suicide, including by philosophers Kant, Mill (the grandfather of modern liberalism), Camus, and as far back as Plato. Setting aside whether the issue is "wrong' or "permissible," all I was trying to do in the article was emphasize the non-legal aspect of death and dying for people to ponder - namely, of approaching the end of one's life and the possibility of God's existence.
